qa.recommendation: Leave the owner as it is. The Consumers Energy purchase of this plant did not happen.
qa.note: CMS Energy and Consumers Energy signed a purchase agreement for Dearborn Industrial Generation in June 2021 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/201533/000110465921084502/tm2120427d1_8k.htm). A press release from the Environmental Law and Policy Center on the 2022 Consumers resource plan settlement (https://elpc.org/news/michigan-energy-regulators-approve-broadly-supported-settlement-on-consumers-energys-long-term-resource-plan/) says the settlement precludes Consumers from buying the plant. In the CMS Energy second quarter 2026 outlook (https://s26.q4cdn.com/888045447/files/doc_financials/2026/q2/CMS-Energy-Second-Quarter-2026-Results-Outlook.pdf), CMS says it keeps Dearborn Industrial Generation inside its NorthStar Clean Energy business. The September 2026 EIA table still lists Dearborn Industrial Gen Inc as the owner. I found no document showing a closed sale to Consumers in 2025, so the brief's premise that U-21090 records that sale was not borne out. I could not read the Michigan Public Service Commission docket directly. The owner company is a CMS NorthStar subsidiary, which a researcher may want to confirm in a CMS annual report.

qa.recommendation: GEM should not hold a unit for the 271 MW project. It was never built and its application was withdrawn in January 2018, before the 2020 start of tracking for cancelled units.
qa.note: A CMS Energy press release from January 29, 2018 (https://www.cmsenergy.com/investor-relations/news-releases/news-release-details/2018/Dearborn-Industrial-Generation-Plant-Rescinds-Expansion-Permit-Request-from-DEQ/default.aspx) says the plant withdrew its request for a new unit expansion air permit. That is probably the project on the Sierra Club list. The release gives no megawatt figure, so the 271 MW size is not confirmed. The three turbines and three boilers in the 2023 permit are the existing plant, with no new unit.
